ui.helpIntroPurpose:
Solar Time is a web-based solar-system clock that presents the current time and planetary motion.
It was created as a screen saver to enjoy whenever you want a brief break from work or study.
ui.helpIntroExperience:
Enjoy the solar system with calming background music,
and use the camera to create your own view of the cosmos.
ui.helpIntroDesktop: This program is optimized for desktop PC environments.
ui.helpFeatureSolar: Take a closer look at planets and major moons with 4K textures.
ui.helpFeatureTime:
View local time across different regions and adjust simulation speed,
then explore eclipses and planetary alignments.
ui.helpFeatureMusic:
Enjoy calming background music while hiding the interface
for a more immersive experience in the cosmos.
ui.helpFeatureTimer:
Set an alarm or schedule your Windows PC to shut down.
Scheduled shutdown requires a separate Windows helper installation.

ui.basicHelp: Left-click and drag to rotate the view, use the mouse wheel to zoom in or out, and middle-click and drag to pan. Double-click a body to follow it up close. Use the left and right arrow keys to select the previous or next body in the footer list; if tracking is active, it continues with the new target. Press 0 to return to the default view. Use the button below Default View on the right to switch the wheel between flat zoom and true camera travel.
ui.timeHelp: The upper clock follows the real local time of the selected language and region. Turn off Real time below to adjust simulation speed in hours, days or years. The ranges are 1 minute–24 hours, 1–365 days, and 1–20 years per second.
ui.orbitHelp: Planets move on elliptical orbits, faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion. Moon and Europa are children of Earth and Jupiter, with positions calculated for the simulation time and eccentricities of 0.05 and 0.01. Long-term perturbations and minute distance changes are omitted, so this is not a precision ephemeris for observation, navigation or eclipse prediction.

polaris: The brightest star in Ursa Minor lies close to Earth's north celestial pole. It appears almost stationary and helps observers find north.
ursa-major: This large northern constellation includes the Big Dipper. Lines extend from the dipper into the bear's body and legs.
ursa-minor: Polaris marks the end of this small dipper's handle. Kochab and Pherkad form its outer bowl.
cassiopeia: Five bright stars form a W or M, depending on the viewing angle. It lies roughly opposite the Big Dipper across Polaris.
orion: Three aligned belt stars make Orion easy to recognise. Red Betelgeuse contrasts with blue-white Rigel; Orion is prominent on winter evenings in Korea.
scorpius: Red Antares leads into a long body and hooked tail. Visible in Korea's southern summer sky, its sting is marked by Shaula and Lesath.
leo: A sickle-shaped head near Regulus and a triangular body outline the lion. Denebola marks the tail; Leo is prominent on spring evenings in Korea.
cygnus: The swan's neck and wings form the Northern Cross. Deneb belongs to the Summer Triangle, while Albireo marks the head.
taurus: Orange Aldebaran, a V-shaped face and two long horns identify Taurus. Aldebaran lies in front of the Hyades cluster, rather than within it.
aries: Hamal, Sheratan and Mesarthim form a short curved chain. This zodiac constellation historically marked the beginning of spring.
gemini: Castor and Pollux mark the twins' heads. Two branching chains of stars form their bodies in this zodiac constellation.
cancer: A faint Y-shaped zodiac constellation around Asellus Borealis and Asellus Australis. The Beehive Cluster helps locate it under dark skies.
virgo: Blue-white Spica anchors this broad zodiac constellation. Between Leo and Libra, it is prominent in the southern sky on spring evenings in Korea.
libra: Zubeneschamali and Zubenelgenubi frame the scales. Its stars were once regarded as the claws of Scorpius.
sagittarius: Stars near Kaus Australis and Nunki form the familiar Teapot. The centre of the Milky Way lies beyond this zodiac constellation.
capricornus: A low, broad wedge extends between Algedi and Deneb Algedi. This faint zodiac constellation is often recognised by its triangular outline.
aquarius: Long streams of stars extend south from Sadalsuud and Sadalmelik. Connecting lines help reveal this widely spread zodiac constellation.
pisces: Two fish are linked by long cords meeting at Alrescha. Their faint outline spans a broad area near the celestial equator.
pegasus: Alpheratz, Algenib, Markab and Scheat form the Great Square. Chains extend into the neck and legs; it is prominent in Korea's autumn sky.
andromeda: A chain leads from Alpheratz through Mirach to Almach. Nearby lies the Andromeda Galaxy, visible to the unaided eye under dark skies.
crux: Acrux and Gacrux form the long axis; Mimosa and Imai form the crossbar. This compact Southern Cross helps observers find south.
sun: A star made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Fusion in its core releases energy as hot plasma and light.
mercury: A rocky planet with an unusually large metallic core. Its water survives mainly as ice in permanently shadowed polar craters.
venus: A silicate-rock planet beneath a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and sulfuric-acid clouds; liquid water is absent from the surface.
earth: A planet of silicate rock and a metallic core. Liquid-water oceans cover most of its surface, beneath a nitrogen- and oxygen-rich atmosphere.
moon: Earth’s rocky, silicate-rich natural satellite. Water occurs mainly as ice in permanently shadowed polar soil and craters.
mars: A rocky planet reddened by iron-oxide dust. Most known water remains as ice in the polar caps and subsurface.
jupiter: A gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface—only deep atmosphere, cloud layers, and giant storms.
europa: A Galilean moon covered by a water-ice crust. A vast, likely salty liquid ocean may lie beneath the ice.
saturn: A gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Its rings are dominated by water ice mixed with rock and dust.
uranus: An ice giant with hydrogen and helium above a deep interior rich in water-, ammonia-, and methane-bearing material; it also has a tipped axis and faint rings.
neptune: An ice giant with hydrogen and helium above water-, ammonia-, and methane-rich material. Atmospheric methane contributes to its blue appearance.
pluto: A dwarf planet of rock and water ice, with a surface coated in nitrogen, methane, and carbon-monoxide ices.
big-dipper: An asterism formed by seven bright stars in Ursa Major. Its dipper-shaped outline is a classic guide to the northern sky, and the line from Merak through Dubhe points toward Polaris.
